outline.title: Does a Zero-Parameter Identity Skip Change Final Error in a Shallow MLP? A Matched-Arm Test on sklearn-digits
outline.question: In a shallow ReLU MLP on sklearn-digits, does a zero-parameter identity skip path change final validation error relative to a weight-identical plain MLP, once parameters, initial weights, minibatch order, step count and a shared learning rate are matched?
outline.nugget: Moving from the lower to the higher shared learning rate lowered error more in the plain arm than in the identity arm. The plain-arm paired difference (higher minus lower rate) has mean -0.93936, with eighteen seeds lower, two tied and none higher. The identity-arm difference has mean -0.330395, with fourteen lower, three tied and three higher. All four protocol arms scored below the depth-one full-batch reference arm at 4.2454.
contributions: At the lower shared learning rate, over twenty paired seeds, the plain arm scored 3.6363 and the identity-skip arm 2.906. The paired difference (plain minus identity) has mean 0.73037, median 0.6945 and seed SD 0.562533. The identity arm was lower on seventeen seeds, tied on three and higher on none.

At the higher shared learning rate, over twenty paired seeds, the plain arm scored 2.697 and the identity-skip arm 2.5756. The paired difference (plain minus identity) has mean 0.121405, median 0.0 and seed SD 0.532522. The identity arm was lower on seven seeds, tied on ten and higher on three.

Moving from the lower to the higher shared learning rate lowered error more in the plain arm than in the identity arm. The plain-arm paired difference (higher minus lower rate) has mean -0.93936, with eighteen seeds lower, two tied and none higher. The identity-arm difference has mean -0.330395, with fourteen lower, three tied and three higher. All four protocol arms scored below the depth-one full-batch reference arm at 4.2454.

Judged by the registered rule, the protocol neither supports nor falsifies H1. At the higher learning rate the mean paired difference lies inside the registered margin, but the engine recorded no interval, so equivalence is not established. At the lower learning rate the mean paired difference already exceeds the margin, so the registered prediction fails there. The registered one-rate attribution cannot be applied, because it presupposes an interval that was not computed.

With the identity path held fixed, reshuffled minibatch SGD with warmup and cosine decay gave five-seed means of 2.7841 and 2.7838 for two warmup fractions, against 3.758 for full-batch training. Every seed was lower in both minibatch runs. Three-seed runs of the two minibatch implementations scored 2.5495 and 2.5491. The change bundles step count, gradient noise and learning-rate schedule, so it cannot be attributed to any one of them.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.purpose: Report a two-point descriptive contrast over 20 paired seeds on sklearn-digits. At lr 0.02 the mean paired gap is 0.73 pp, with the identity arm lower on 17 seeds, tied on 3 and higher on none. At lr 0.05 it is 0.12 pp, with 7 lower, 10 tied and 3 higher. No interval was computed. Present this as an interaction between skip path and learning rate, not as a trend. Give the matched-arm design and note that the registered verdict is inconclusive.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.purpose: Define the task, then frame the gap only through the approved related-work statements. FractalNet and the shallow-paths account concern ultra-deep or normalised residual networks. RoR reports gains without a matched no-shortcut ablation. Hourglass compares skip placement on generative tasks, not skip against no skip. Our move is to isolate one zero-parameter skip with a parameter-identical control at shallow depth and with no normalisation. State the evidence as the two-rate descriptive contrast over 20 seeds: 0.73 pp at lr 0.02 against 0.12 pp at lr 0.05, with no interval. Describe it in interaction terms: the two arms differ in learning-rate sensitivity. Then list the contribution bullets.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.purpose: Group prior work by mechanism, giving the exact difference from this study for each group. Optimisation-at-initialisation accounts: the shallow-paths account and shortcut theory. Whether the identity path is needed: FractalNet. Shortcut-adding architectures: RoR, Hourglass and capsule networks. The differences are shallow depth, no normalisation, and a zero-parameter matched skip compared against no skip.

sections.heading: Setup and Protocol
sections.purpose: Give enough detail to reimplement the study. Cover the data, split and metric; the protocol architecture and arms; optimisation and paired seeding; the registered prediction and rule; and the deviations from the pre-registered plan.

sections.heading: Exploration Runs (Earlier in Time)
sections.purpose: Describe the earlier exploration configurations and mark them as exploration only, separate from the protocol. These cover the full-batch identity reparametrisation, the fidelity levels, and the minibatch, weight-decay and width settings.

sections.heading: Results: Matched Protocol
sections.purpose: At each of the two shared learning rates, test whether the skip changes final error. Report paired means, medians, seed SD and win/tie/loss counts, all descriptive and without intervals. Then report how each arm's error changed between the two rates, framed as an interaction between path and rate rather than a monotone trend. End with the registered verdict.

sections.heading: Results: Exploration
sections.purpose: Report three groups of exploration results. First, the unreplicated single-seed skip contrasts, including the deterministic agreement of the two identity-path scripts. Second, the bundled minibatch gain over full-batch training. Third, the weight-decay and width changes, which cannot be attributed to a single factor.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.purpose: Separate what was measured from the optimisation-speed hypothesis, which is untested here and stated with hedging. That hypothesis would fit both the larger gap at lr 0.02 and the identity arm's lower sensitivity to learning rate. Name the competing account that the plain arm is under-converged at the lower rate. Note that two rates cannot establish a trend.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.purpose: Tie each limitation to a scope boundary, and say for each whether it undermines the core claim. The boundaries are: no interval or TOST, and 20 seeds instead of 30; a coarse metric on about 288 validation images; export equivalence; missing diagnostic logs; no learning curves; coupled seeds and folds; the difference in initial function between arms; the exploration reparametrisation; exploration changes that cannot be attributed to one factor; a single dataset; provenance; uncounted failed runs; and the interaction between path and learning rate.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.purpose: Restate the question. The answer within scope is a descriptive two-rate contrast on sklearn-digits over 20 seeds: 0.73 pp at lr 0.02 against 0.12 pp at lr 0.05, with no interval, and a registered verdict that is inconclusive. Give one limitation: no learning curves. Close with the next step: matched-step learning curves, interval estimates and more learning rates.

issues.target: Section 2 (Introduction): 'the gap: prior skip studies use deep networks and no matched control'
issues.issue: This gap statement reaches beyond the approved related-work statements. related_ror supports 'no matched no-shortcut ablation' only for RoR. related_hourglass explicitly describes parameter-matched designs, which contradicts 'no matched control' as a blanket claim. No statement says prior skip studies in general lack matched controls.
issues.suggestion: Frame the gap only through what the cited statements say: deep or ultra-deep settings (related_fractalnet, related_shallow_paths), no matched ablation in RoR (related_ror), and skip placement rather than skip versus no skip in Hourglass (related_hourglass). Drop the general 'no matched control' claim.

issues.target: Section 2 (Introduction) headline: 'the skip benefit shrinks as learning rate rises'; Section 1 and Section 10: 'the skip effect depends on learning rate'
issues.issue: Only two shared rates (0.02, 0.05) were run, with no interval or test (limit_1). 'Shrinks as learning rate rises' implies a monotone trend across rates, which the evidence cannot support. 'Depends on' is offered as a finding, although the comparison is descriptive and the 0.05 near-tie cannot be called equivalence (claim_protocol_verdict).
issues.suggestion: State the two-point contrast in the scope it was measured in: a mean paired gap of 0.73 pp (17/3/0) at lr 0.02 against 0.12 pp (7/10/3) at lr 0.05, over 20 seeds on sklearn-digits, descriptive with no interval. Use the interaction wording of limit_17 instead of a trend claim.

issues.issue: The headline claims carry no scope boundary. limit_1 (no interval, 20 instead of 30 seeds) and limit_14 (one dataset, one depth, one width family) are not attached to the abstract or the conclusion's main sentence.
issues.suggestion: Add limit_1 and limit_14 to the Abstract and Conclusion evidence, so the inconclusive and descriptive status and the single-dataset scope appear next to the headline.

issues.issue: This is an exploration result, it is bundled and unattributable, and it does not bear on the skip question. Listing it as a contribution beside the protocol results inflates its role.
issues.suggestion: Move it to Exploration results only, or mark it explicitly as an exploration observation, citing limit_10.

issues.issue: The discussion names the under-convergence alternative but omits the initial-function difference (limit_7), another confound for the lr-dependent gap.
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_7 alongside limit_5 when presenting competing accounts.

issues.target: Section 2 Introduction — gap framing ('prior skip studies use deep networks and no matched control')
issues.issue: This gap is broader than any approved statement supports. related_ror says only that RoR lacks a matched no-shortcut ablation. related_fractalnet describes FractalNet as a comparison without identity connections, which works against 'no matched control'. related_shallow_paths and related_shortcut_theory say nothing about control design. As written, the introduction would assert an unsupported claim about prior work in general.
issues.suggestion: State the gap only through the approved differentiators: prior work studies ultra-deep or normalised residual networks (related_fractalnet, related_shallow_paths), RoR reports gains without a matched ablation (related_ror), and this study isolates one zero-parameter skip with a parameter-identical control at shallow depth and with no normalisation. Drop the blanket 'no matched control' wording.

issues.target: Sections 1, 2, 10 — 'the skip benefit shrinks as learning rate rises'
issues.issue: Only two shared rates were run. 'Shrinks as learning rate rises' implies a trend that two points cannot establish. The evidence also sits beside a registered verdict that is inconclusive (claim_protocol_verdict) and a declared path-by-learning-rate interaction (limit_17).
issues.suggestion: Frame the headline as a two-point contrast: a large paired gap at the lower of two shared rates (claim_protocol_lr002) and a near-tie with ten ties at the higher (claim_protocol_lr005). Cite limit_17 where the interaction is named.

issues.issue: The question asks whether the skip changes final error. The nugget (claim_lr_sensitivity) instead answers how each arm responds to learning rate. Its last sentence, about the reference arm, also adds a second message. The direct answer to the question lives in claim_protocol_lr002 and claim_protocol_lr005, which the abstract already leads with. Nugget and abstract therefore pull in slightly different directions.
issues.suggestion: Keep claim_lr_sensitivity as the nugget, but have the abstract and introduction say explicitly that the nugget is the answer to the question: the skip's effect on final error is a learning-rate interaction. Alternatively, ask the author for a nugget statement that combines the two per-rate results.

issues.target: Contributions — third bullet duplicates the nugget
issues.issue: The third contribution repeats the nugget verbatim.
issues.suggestion: Drop it from the bullets, or state in the plan that the nugget is listed as the central contribution and not repeated.

issues.issue: The minibatch-versus-full-batch result holds the identity path fixed, so it does not bear on the skip question. Listing it as a headline contribution dilutes the single question.
issues.suggestion: Remove it from the contributions and the introduction, and report it only in Section 7 as exploration context explaining why the protocol uses minibatch SGD.

issues.target: Section order — Section 5 (Exploration setup) placed before Section 6 (Protocol results)
issues.issue: The exploration configuration sits between the protocol setup and the protocol results. The reader must absorb setup that is irrelevant to the main answer before reaching it.
issues.suggestion: Merge Section 5 into Section 7, so the exploration setup is followed directly by its results, after the protocol results. Alternatively, move Section 5 to just before Section 7.

issues.target: Section 7 Results: Exploration — missing caveat statements
issues.issue: The single-seed skip contrasts use a W = I + W' reparametrisation, not the protocol's additive skip. Without limit_8 beside them, readers may read them as corroborating the protocol. Likewise limit_9 (registration not logged) belongs with claim_fullbatch_lr01_seed0.
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_8 and limit_9 in Section 7 next to the claims they qualify, as well as in Section 9.

issues.target: Section 6 Results: Matched Protocol — tie interpretation
issues.issue: There are ten ties at the higher rate and three at the lower. These are hard to read without the single-image granularity and the coupling of seeds and folds.
issues.suggestion: Add setup_val_size or limit_2, and limit_6, to the evidence for Section 6, so the medians of 0.0 and the tie counts are interpreted at the point where they appear.

issues.issue: The plan says to name the competing under-convergence account but does not cite limit_5, the statement that names it explicitly.
issues.suggestion: Add limit_5 to the Section 8 evidence. Consider also limit_7 (the arms differ in initial function, and learning rate was shared rather than tuned), which is relevant to interpreting the interaction.

issues.issue: The statement itself calls the capsule paper peripheral and records no abstract. It does not serve the question.
issues.suggestion: Omit related_capsule.

issues.target: Section 2 (Introduction), gap sentence 'prior skip studies use deep networks and no matched control'
issues.issue: No approved statement supports this generalisation. related_hourglass describes parameter-matched designs, and related_shortcut_theory covers a two-layer setting. Only related_ror records a missing matched no-shortcut ablation, and that statement is not cited here. As written, the gap claims more than the evidence and partly contradicts it.
issues.suggestion: Narrow the gap to what the approved related-work statements say. RoR lacks a matched no-shortcut ablation. FractalNet and shallow_paths concern ultra-deep or normalised networks. Hourglass compares skip placement on generative tasks. Cite related_ror, related_fractalnet and related_hourglass in the Introduction evidence, and drop the blanket 'no matched control'.

issues.target: Section 2 (Introduction), 'the skip benefit shrinks as learning rate rises'
issues.issue: Only two shared learning rates were run. 'Shrinks as learning rate rises' implies a trend that two points cannot establish. No interval exists for either paired difference (limit_1).
issues.suggestion: Phrase it as a contrast between the two rates tested, 0.02 versus 0.05, as claim_protocol_lr002/lr005 do. Keep it descriptive.

issues.target: Section 1 (Abstract), 'the skip effect depends on learning rate'
issues.issue: This reads as an established interaction. The evidence is descriptive mean paired differences with no interval or test, on 20 instead of 30 seeds. The higher-rate difference (mean 0.12, median 0, SD 0.53) is within single-image resolution.
issues.suggestion: Add limit_1 (and optionally limit_2) to the Abstract evidence, so the abstract states that the comparison is descriptive with no interval.

issues.issue: The exploration identity path (W = I + W' inside the ReLU) is a different intervention from the protocol's additive skip. That caveat appears only in Limitations (limit_8). A reader comparing Sections 6 and 7 may read the exploration contrasts as the same skip.
issues.suggestion: Place limit_8 next to setup_explore_identity in Section 5 or at the start of Section 7, and cite limit_9 alongside claim_fullbatch_lr01_seed0.

issues.issue: Both statements report the same lr 0.1 seed-zero tie of 4.5139, so the plan risks repeating it.
issues.suggestion: Use claim_skip_effect_unresolved for the contrast and claim_fullbatch_lr01_seed0 only for the script-determinism point and the plain arm's three-seed mean.

issues.issue: The logistic-regression baseline (3.8%) and the reference arm (4.2454) are introduced in Setup but not tied to the protocol results. Readers cannot easily see that both arms beat the strongest simple baseline.
issues.suggestion: Cite setup_baseline and setup_arm_reference in Section 6 next to the arm means.

issues.target: Section 6, coupling of seeds and folds
issues.issue: Win/tie/loss counts and seed SDs are reported over seed-fold pairs that may be dependent (limit_6), and many differences are single-image changes (limit_2).
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_2 and limit_6 in Section 6 where the counts and SDs are presented, not only in Limitations.

points.claim: In a shallow ReLU MLP on sklearn-digits, does a zero-parameter identity skip path change final validation error relative to a weight-identical plain MLP, once parameters, initial weights, minibatch order, step count and a shared learning rate are matched?

A frozen protocol trained a two-block, width-128 MLP with and without a zero-parameter identity skip. The two arms were paired on twenty seeds, with identical initial weights, minibatch order and step count, at each of two shared learning rates. A depth-one default recipe served as the anchor arm. The engine reports per-seed paired differences in validation top-1 error. These are judged descriptively against the registered ±0.5 pp prediction. Earlier exploration runs come first in time and are reported as exploration only: single-seed full-batch skip-versus-plain contrasts, a switch to minibatch SGD, and weight-decay and width changes. No new experiments were run.

At the lower shared learning rate, over twenty paired seeds, the plain arm scored 3.6363 and the identity-skip arm 2.906. The paired difference (plain minus identity) has mean 0.73037, median 0.6945 and seed SD 0.562533. The identity arm was lower on seventeen seeds, tied on three and higher on none.

At the higher shared learning rate, over twenty paired seeds, the plain arm scored 2.697 and the identity-skip arm 2.5756. The paired difference (plain minus identity) has mean 0.121405, median 0.0 and seed SD 0.532522. The identity arm was lower on seven seeds, tied on ten and higher on three.

Moving from the lower to the higher shared learning rate lowered error more in the plain arm than in the identity arm. The plain-arm paired difference (higher minus lower rate) has mean -0.93936, with eighteen seeds lower, two tied and none higher. The identity-arm difference has mean -0.330395, with fourteen lower, three tied and three higher. All four protocol arms scored below the depth-one full-batch reference arm at 4.2454.

Judged by the registered rule, the protocol neither supports nor falsifies H1. At the higher learning rate the mean paired difference lies inside the registered margin, but the engine recorded no interval, so equivalence is not established. At the lower learning rate the mean paired difference already exceeds the margin, so the registered prediction fails there. The registered one-rate attribution cannot be applied, because it presupposes an interval that was not computed.

Data are sklearn-digits 8x8 images scaled by 1/16. A fixed stratified 20% test split is held out, and the other 80% is cut into 5 stratified folds; the assigned fold is the validation split and the rest is training data.
Each validation fold has about 288 images, so one misclassified image is about 0.35 pp.
The metric is val_top1_err: top-1 error in percent on the validation fold. It is computed by the frozen scorer, which rebuilds a Linear/ReLU stack from the saved state_dict.
The profile records a logistic-regression baseline of 3.8 percent validation error.
Protocol architecture: input projection 64->128 with ReLU, then two blocks h=ReLU(W h+b), then a 10-way head. This equals build_model with depth=3 and hidden=128.
Arm plain_lr005 runs train.py v7 with SKIP=False at lr 0.05: the plain block h=ReLU(W h+b).
Arm plain_lr002 runs train.py v7 with SKIP=False and differs from plain_lr005 only in using lr 0.02.

Arm resid_lr005 runs train.py v8, which differs from v7 only in SKIP=True, so h_{l+1} = h_l + ReLU(W_l h_l + b_l), at lr 0.05. Weights are exported as an equivalent width-256 stack, and the run asserts max_abs_diff < 1e-3.
Arm resid_lr002 runs train.py v8 with SKIP=True and differs from resid_lr005 only in using lr 0.02.
The reference arm runs the unmodified train.py v2 at depth 1 and hidden 128, full-batch, with lr 0.05 for 120 epochs. It anchors the paired differences and is not part of the skip contrast.
Protocol training: minibatch SGD with batch 64, momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0001 and cross-entropy loss for 120 epochs, at a constant learning rate with no schedule.

Protocol seeding: torch and numpy are seeded with the seed index, and weights use default PyTorch Linear initialisation via build_model. Per-epoch permutations come from a torch Generator seeded with 1000003 plus the seed, identical across paired arms.
Every protocol arm ran seeds 1 to 20 at verify fidelity with a 180-second budget per run. Folds cycle through 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, and each seed index uses the same fold in every arm.

The selected idea pre-registered a paired TOST at α = 0.05 with a 0.5 pp margin on final error over 30 paired seeds. Per-arm lr was to be chosen from {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on a 20% inner split, with a shared-lr robustness sweep.

Registered prediction: at lr=0.05, the paired mean difference (resid_lr005 - plain_lr005) in final val_top1_err has magnitude under 0.5 pp and its 90% interval lies inside [-0.5, +0.5] pp. The same holds for the lr=0.02 pair, and both arms reach roughly 2-4% error.

Registered outcome rule: H1 is falsified only if the paired 90% interval lies entirely outside [-0.5, +0.5] pp at both lr=0.05 and lr=0.02. An effect at one lr only is attributed to lr sensitivity. An interval straddling a margin boundary is inconclusive.

The run protocol dropped per-arm lr tuning and reduced the shared-lr grid to two values, 0.05 and 0.02. It used 20 seeds instead of 30 and computed descriptive paired mean differences instead of TOST.
Exploration full-batch runs train depth 2 at hidden 128 with full-batch SGD at momentum 0.9 and weight decay 0.0001 for 120 epochs, one step per epoch.

The exploration identity path reparametrises each square hidden Linear as W_eff = I + W'. This adds no parameters, and the reparametrisation is folded back into plain weights after training so the frozen scorer evaluates the trained function.
Full-batch exploration runs exp_0001, exp_0002, exp_0004 and exp_0005 used lr 0.05. Runs exp_0003, exp_0006, exp_0007 and exp_0008 used lr 0.1.
exp_0007 runs train.py v3 with SKIP hard-coded on, and exp_0008 runs v1 with a skip flag defaulting to 1. Both run at lr 0.1 and otherwise perform the same computation.
Exploration runs seed torch and numpy with the run seed and use default PyTorch Linear initialisation via build_model.
Exploration fidelities: smoke uses seed 0 on fold 0, verify uses seeds 0-2 on folds 0-2, and full uses seeds 0-4 on folds 0-4.

Exploration minibatch runs use SGD with momentum 0.9 and cross-entropy loss at batch 64. Batches are reshuffled each epoch by a torch Generator seeded with the run seed, under a linear warmup then cosine decay, with warmup_frac 0.03 or 0.05.

Minibatch runs exp_0012, exp_0013, exp_0016 and exp_0017 used lr 0.05, depth 2, hidden 128, weight_decay 0.0001 and 120 epochs with the identity path on. The weight-decay and width arms exp_0021 to exp_0024 also used lr 0.05; weight_decay 0.0004 was the highest value run.

The weight-decay and width arms all use the warmup-0.05 minibatch script: exp_0024 at hidden 128 with weight_decay 0.0004, exp_0023 at hidden 128 with 0.0004, exp_0021 at hidden 256 with 0.0004, and exp_0022 at hidden 256 with 0.0003.

The weight-decay and width arms exp_0021 to exp_0024 used depth 2 and 120 epochs. Runs exp_0014 and exp_0015 used lr 0.05, depth 2, hidden 128, weight_decay 0.0001, 120 epochs and warmup_frac 0.03 with the identity path on.

The single-seed full-batch exploration contrasts point the same way or not at all. At the lower exploration learning rate, the identity-path arm scored 3.4722 against 5.2083 for the plain arm. At the higher exploration learning rate, both arms scored 4.5139. That is one seed-zero contrast favouring the identity path and one exact tie, and neither is replicated, so these runs leave the skip effect unresolved.

At the higher full-batch exploration learning rate on seed zero, the plain arm and two identity-path runs all scored 4.5139. The two identity-path runs use scripts that perform the same computation and differ only in how the skip is switched on, so their agreement shows deterministic code, not independent replication. The plain arm's three-seed mean at this rate was 3.8235. No identity-path run with more than one seed exists at this rate.

Raising weight decay to the top of its range in the minibatch regime gave a five-seed mean of 2.575 against 2.7838. Seeds zero, two and four fell (2.4306 to 2.0833, 2.439 to 2.0906, 4.5296 to 4.1812); seeds one and three were unchanged. Changing only the warmup fraction moves seed zero between 2.4306 and 2.0833 and seed two between 2.439 and 2.7875. Those are changes of the same size, so the drop cannot be attributed to weight decay.

At matched weight decay on three seeds, the wider network scored 2.3176 against 2.3172 for the narrower one. It was lower on seed zero (1.7361 versus 2.0833), equal on seed one (2.7778) and higher on seed two (2.439 versus 2.0906). The width contrast is mixed with no net change. A wider run that also lowered weight decay gave identical per-seed scores of 1.7361, 2.7778 and 2.439.

One explanation fits the pattern: the identity path speeds optimisation under the fixed step budget, so its advantage is largest where the plain arm trains more slowly, at the lower learning rate. The same account would explain why the identity arm is less sensitive to learning rate. This explanation is untested. No validation curves or training-loss logs are in the record, and a slower-converging plain arm and a genuine endpoint effect would produce the same final-error data.

The two arms differ in learning-rate sensitivity, so the path and the learning rate interact. The registered rule, which attributes an effect at one learning rate to learning-rate sensitivity, cannot cleanly separate the two.

The engine computed only mean paired differences. No TOST, no 90% interval and no bootstrap were computed, and the protocol used twenty seeds rather than the registered thirty. The verdict is therefore descriptive and cannot declare equivalence at either learning rate.
The validation fold has about 288 images, so one image moves error by about 0.35 pp. Many paired differences are exact ties or single-image changes, which is close to the registered margin.

Residual arms are scored through an exported width-256 Linear/ReLU stack that re-expresses the trained width-128 residual network. Equivalence is asserted in-script, but float summation order may flip rare ties.

The DIAG logs are not in the dossier: init and data-order hashes, step counts, skip activation, export max_abs_diff and activation norms. The protocol's void conditions therefore cannot be checked from the record.

No per-epoch validation curves exist, so speed cannot be separated from endpoint error. The optimisation-speed explanation remains a hypothesis. A competing explanation is that the plain arm is under-converged at the lower learning rate.
Seeds and folds are coupled: each seed is paired with a fold in a fixed cycle, so seed and fold effects cannot be separated and the twenty observations may be dependent.

Within the protocol, the residual arm differs from the plain arm in its initial function, because the skip is active from step zero, and not only in its trajectory. Learning rate was shared rather than tuned per arm.

The exploration identity path sits inside the ReLU as a weight reparametrisation (W = I + W'). It is not the protocol's additive skip, and weight decay pulls its weights toward identity rather than zero.

The two seed-zero identity-path runs at the higher full-batch learning rate agree because the code is identical and deterministic. Neither script logs parametrisation registration; that it took effect is inferred from the code and from the lower-rate difference.

The minibatch-versus-full-batch gain is descriptive across five paired seed/fold pairs with no significance test. No full-batch control with a matched step count separates gradient noise from step count.
The weight-decay per-seed changes match warmup-only changes in size. No training error was logged, so the overfitting premise behind the weight-decay change is untested.
Width is isolated only at weight decay 0.0004, on three seeds (exp_0021 versus exp_0023). exp_0022 changes width and weight decay jointly, and no five-seed width result exists.
Identical per-seed scores at weight decay 0.0003 and 0.0004 may be coincidences of the coarse metric. No saved artifact config was checked to confirm which weight decay was applied.
Results come from one dataset, one depth and one width family. Nothing here generalises to deeper networks, other datasets or normalised residual networks.
Current engine source is not proof of historical execution. Legacy exploration records may lack code, data or environment snapshots.

The record does not count runs that failed, were killed under the time budget, timed out or were voided. It lists each recorded run as kept or discarded and gives the training attempts of each protocol arm; nothing further can be recovered.

Arm plain_lr005 runs train.py v7 with SKIP=False at lr 0.05: the plain block h=ReLU(W h+b).
Arm plain_lr002 runs train.py v7 with SKIP=False and differs from plain_lr005 only in using lr 0.02.

Arm resid_lr005 runs train.py v8, which differs from v7 only in SKIP=True, so h_{l+1} = h_l + ReLU(W_l h_l + b_l), at lr 0.05. Weights are exported as an equivalent width-256 stack, and the run asserts max_abs_diff < 1e-3.
Arm resid_lr002 runs train.py v8 with SKIP=True and differs from resid_lr005 only in using lr 0.02.
The reference arm runs the unmodified train.py v2 at depth 1 and hidden 128, full-batch, with lr 0.05 for 120 epochs. It anchors the paired differences and is not part of the skip contrast.
Protocol training: minibatch SGD with batch 64, momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0001 and cross-entropy loss for 120 epochs, at a constant learning rate with no schedule.

Protocol seeding: torch and numpy are seeded with the seed index, and weights use default PyTorch Linear initialisation via build_model. Per-epoch permutations come from a torch Generator seeded with 1000003 plus the seed, identical across paired arms.
Every protocol arm ran seeds 1 to 20 at verify fidelity with a 180-second budget per run. Folds cycle through 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, and each seed index uses the same fold in every arm.

The selected idea pre-registered a paired TOST at α = 0.05 with a 0.5 pp margin on final error over 30 paired seeds. Per-arm lr was to be chosen from {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on a 20% inner split, with a shared-lr robustness sweep.

Registered outcome rule: H1 is falsified only if the paired 90% interval lies entirely outside [-0.5, +0.5] pp at both lr=0.05 and lr=0.02. An effect at one lr only is attributed to lr sensitivity. An interval straddling a margin boundary is inconclusive.

The run protocol dropped per-arm lr tuning and reduced the shared-lr grid to two values, 0.05 and 0.02. It used 20 seeds instead of 30 and computed descriptive paired mean differences instead of TOST.
Exploration full-batch runs train depth 2 at hidden 128 with full-batch SGD at momentum 0.9 and weight decay 0.0001 for 120 epochs, one step per epoch.

Full-batch exploration runs exp_0001, exp_0002, exp_0004 and exp_0005 used lr 0.05. Runs exp_0003, exp_0006, exp_0007 and exp_0008 used lr 0.1.

The registered one-rate attribution cannot be applied, because it presupposes an interval that was not computed.

That is one seed-zero contrast favouring the identity path and one exact tie, and neither is replicated, so these runs leave the skip effect unresolved.

The two identity-path runs use scripts that perform the same computation and differ only in how the skip is switched on, so their agreement shows deterministic code, not independent replication. The plain arm's three-seed mean at this rate was 3.8235. No identity-path run with more than one seed exists at this rate.

Every seed was lower in both minibatch runs. Three-seed runs of the two minibatch implementations scored 2.5495 and 2.5491. The change bundles step count, gradient noise and learning-rate schedule, so it cannot be attributed to any one of them.

Raising weight decay to the top of its range in the minibatch regime gave a five-seed mean of 2.575 against 2.7838. Seeds zero, two and four fell (2.4306 to 2.0833, 2.439 to 2.0906, 4.5296 to 4.1812); seeds one and three were unchanged. The same account would explain why the identity arm is less sensitive to learning rate. This explanation is untested. No validation curves or training-loss logs are in the record, and a slower-converging plain arm and a genuine endpoint effect would produce the same final-error data.

The two arms differ in learning-rate sensitivity, so the path and the learning rate interact. The registered rule, which attributes an effect at one learning rate to learning-rate sensitivity, cannot cleanly separate the two.

The engine computed only mean paired differences. No TOST, no 90% interval and no bootstrap were computed, and the protocol used twenty seeds rather than the registered thirty. The verdict is therefore descriptive and cannot declare equivalence at either learning rate.
The validation fold has about 288 images, so one image moves error by about 0.35 pp. Many paired differences are exact ties or single-image changes, which is close to the registered margin.

Residual arms are scored through an exported width-256 Linear/ReLU stack that re-expresses the trained width-128 residual network. Equivalence is asserted in-script, but float summation order may flip rare ties.

The DIAG logs are not in the dossier: init and data-order hashes, step counts, skip activation, export max_abs_diff and activation norms. The protocol's void conditions therefore cannot be checked from the record.

No per-epoch validation curves exist, so speed cannot be separated from endpoint error. The optimisation-speed explanation remains a hypothesis. A competing explanation is that the plain arm is under-converged at the lower learning rate.
Seeds and folds are coupled: each seed is paired with a fold in a fixed cycle, so seed and fold effects cannot be separated and the twenty observations may be dependent.

Within the protocol, the residual arm differs from the plain arm in its initial function, because the skip is active from step zero, and not only in its trajectory. Learning rate was shared rather than tuned per arm.

The exploration identity path sits inside the ReLU as a weight reparametrisation (W = I + W'). It is not the protocol's additive skip, and weight decay pulls its weights toward identity rather than zero.

The two seed-zero identity-path runs at the higher full-batch learning rate agree because the code is identical and deterministic. Neither script logs parametrisation registration; that it took effect is inferred from the code and from the lower-rate difference.

Results come from one dataset, one depth and one width family. Nothing here generalises to deeper networks, other datasets or normalised residual networks.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.body:
We ask whether, in a shallow ReLU MLP on sklearn-digits, a zero-parameter identity skip path changes final validation error relative to a weight-identical plain MLP once parameters, initial weights, minibatch order, step count and a shared learning rate are matched [scope_question]. A frozen protocol trained a two-block, width-128 MLP with and without the identity skip, pairing the two arms on twenty seeds with identical initial weights, minibatch order and step count at each of two shared learning rates [scope_method]. A depth-one default recipe served as the anchor arm [scope_method]. The engine reports per-seed paired differences in validation top-1 error (lower error is better), and we judge these descriptively against the registered ±0.5 pp prediction [scope_method]. Earlier single-seed full-batch contrasts, a switch to minibatch SGD, and weight-decay and width changes are reported as exploration only, and no new experiments were run [scope_method].

At the lower shared learning rate, the mean paired difference (plain minus identity) is 0.73037, with the identity arm lower on seventeen seeds, tied on three and higher on none [claim_protocol_lr002]. At the higher shared learning rate, the mean paired difference is 0.121405, with the identity arm lower on seven seeds, tied on ten and higher on three [claim_protocol_lr005]. Moving from the lower to the higher shared learning rate lowered error more in the plain arm, with a mean paired change of -0.93936, than in the identity arm, with a mean paired change of -0.330395 [claim_lr_sensitivity]. All four protocol arms scored below the depth-one full-batch reference arm at 4.2454 [claim_lr_sensitivity].

Judged by the registered rule, the protocol neither supports nor falsifies H1 [claim_protocol_verdict]. The lower-rate mean already exceeds the margin, and the higher-rate mean lies inside it with no recorded interval, so equivalence is not established and the registered one-rate attribution cannot be applied [claim_protocol_verdict].

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
We ask whether, in a shallow ReLU MLP on sklearn-digits, a zero-parameter identity skip path changes final validation error relative to a weight-identical plain MLP once parameters, initial weights, minibatch order, step count and a shared learning rate are matched [scope_question].

FractalNet matches ResNets without identity connections in ultra-deep convolutional networks, and we ask the related question of whether the identity path matters at shallow MLP depth with a parameter-identical control [related_fractalnet]. A separate account attributes batch normalisation's benefit in deep ResNets to downscaling the residual branch by a factor of about sqrt(depth), whereas we work at a depth where that factor is near one and use no normalisation [related_shallow_paths].

RoR adds multilevel shortcuts to deep ResNets and reports accuracy gains without a matched no-shortcut ablation, so we isolate a single zero-parameter skip instead [related_ror]. Hourglass MLPs compare skip placement under parameter-matched designs on generative tasks, and we compare skip against no skip on a classification task [related_hourglass].

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.body:
The shallow-paths account attributes the benefit of batch normalisation in deep ResNets to downscaling the residual branch by a factor of about sqrt(depth) [related_shallow_paths]. Our study works at a depth where that factor is near one, and it uses no normalisation [related_shallow_paths]. Shortcut theory proves that, in a stylised two-layer convolutional ResNet, gradient descent with proper normalisation and suitable initialisation avoids a spurious optimum when shortcuts are present [related_shortcut_theory]. We measure only whether a matched zero-parameter skip changes final error in an unnormalised shallow MLP, so we do not test that optimisation mechanism [related_shortcut_theory].

FractalNet matches ResNets without identity connections in ultra-deep convolutional networks [related_fractalnet]. We ask the related question of whether the identity path matters, but at shallow MLP depth and with a parameter-identical control [related_fractalnet].

RoR adds multilevel shortcuts to deep ResNets and reports accuracy gains without a matched no-shortcut ablation [related_ror]. Our study instead isolates a single zero-parameter skip [related_ror]. Hourglass MLPs compare skip placement under parameter-matched designs on generative tasks [related_hourglass]. We compare skip against no skip on a classification task [related_hourglass]. Residual connections have also been applied to train deeper capsule networks [related_capsule]. That work is peripheral to our question, and its record carries no abstract [related_capsule].

sections.heading: Setup and Protocol
sections.body:
Data are sklearn-digits 8x8 images scaled by 1/16 [setup_data]. A fixed stratified 20% test split is held out, and the other 80% is cut into 5 stratified folds [setup_data]. The assigned fold serves as the validation split, and the remaining folds form the training data [setup_data]. Each validation fold has about 288 images, so one misclassified image is about 0.35 pp [setup_val_size]. The metric is val_top1_err, the top-1 error in percent on the validation fold, where lower is better [setup_metric]. The frozen scorer computes it by rebuilding a Linear/ReLU stack from the saved state_dict [setup_metric]. For context, the profile records a logistic-regression baseline of 3.8 percent validation error [setup_baseline].

The protocol architecture is an input projection 64->128 with ReLU, then two blocks h=ReLU(W h+b), then a 10-way head [setup_protocol_arch]. This network equals build_model with depth=3 and hidden=128 [setup_protocol_arch]. Arm plain_lr005 runs train.py v7 with SKIP=False at lr 0.05, which gives the plain block h=ReLU(W h+b) [setup_arm_plain_lr005]. Arm plain_lr002 also runs train.py v7 with SKIP=False and differs from plain_lr005 only in using lr 0.02 [setup_arm_plain_lr002].

Arm resid_lr005 runs train.py v8, which differs from v7 only in SKIP=True, so that h_{l+1} = h_l + ReLU(W_l h_l + b_l), at lr 0.05 [setup_arm_resid_lr005]. Its weights are exported as an equivalent width-256 stack, and the run asserts max_abs_diff < 1e-3 [setup_arm_resid_lr005]. Arm resid_lr002 runs train.py v8 with SKIP=True and differs from resid_lr005 only in using lr 0.02 [setup_arm_resid_lr002]. The reference arm runs the unmodified train.py v2 at depth 1 and hidden 128, full-batch, with lr 0.05 for 120 epochs [setup_arm_reference]. The reference arm anchors the paired differences and is not part of the skip contrast [setup_arm_reference].

Protocol training uses minibatch SGD with batch 64, momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0001 and cross-entropy loss for 120 epochs, at a constant learning rate with no schedule [setup_protocol_optim]. Torch and numpy are seeded with the seed index, and weights use default PyTorch Linear initialisation via build_model [setup_protocol_seeding]. Per-epoch permutations come from a torch Generator seeded with 1000003 plus the seed, so they are identical across paired arms [setup_protocol_seeding]. Every protocol arm ran seeds 1 to 20 at verify fidelity with a 180-second budget per run [setup_protocol_seeds]. Folds cycle through 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, and each seed index uses the same fold in every arm [setup_protocol_seeds].

The selected idea pre-registered a paired TOST at α = 0.05 with a 0.5 pp margin on final error over 30 paired seeds [setup_preregistered_plan]. Under that plan, per-arm lr was to be chosen from {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on a 20% inner split, with a shared-lr robustness sweep [setup_preregistered_plan]. The registered prediction states that at lr=0.05 the paired mean difference (resid_lr005 - plain_lr005) in final val_top1_err has magnitude under 0.5 pp and its 90% interval lies inside [-0.5, +0.5] pp [setup_protocol_prediction]. The prediction states the same for the lr=0.02 pair and expects both arms to reach roughly 2-4% error [setup_protocol_prediction].

The registered outcome rule falsifies H1 only if the paired 90% interval lies entirely outside [-0.5, +0.5] pp at both lr=0.05 and lr=0.02 [setup_protocol_rule]. Under the same rule, an effect at one lr only is attributed to lr sensitivity [setup_protocol_rule]. An interval straddling a margin boundary counts as inconclusive [setup_protocol_rule].

The run protocol deviated from this plan by dropping per-arm lr tuning and reducing the shared-lr grid to two values, 0.05 and 0.02 [setup_protocol_deviations]. It also used 20 seeds instead of 30 and computed descriptive paired mean differences instead of TOST [setup_protocol_deviations].

sections.heading: Exploration Runs (Earlier in Time)
sections.body:
The exploration full-batch runs train depth 2 at hidden 128 with full-batch SGD at momentum 0.9 and weight decay 0.0001 for 120 epochs, taking one step per epoch [setup_explore_fullbatch]. In these runs the identity path reparametrises each square hidden Linear as W_eff = I + W' [setup_explore_identity]. The reparametrisation adds no parameters, and it is folded back into plain weights after training so that the frozen scorer evaluates the trained function [setup_explore_identity].

The full-batch exploration runs used two learning rates: exp_0001, exp_0002, exp_0004 and exp_0005 used lr 0.05, and exp_0003, exp_0006, exp_0007 and exp_0008 used lr 0.1 [setup_explore_lr]. Two of the lr 0.1 runs come from different script versions: exp_0007 runs train.py v3 with SKIP hard-coded on, and exp_0008 runs v1 with a skip flag defaulting to 1 [setup_explore_lr01_scripts]. Both run at lr 0.1 and otherwise perform the same computation [setup_explore_lr01_scripts].

Each exploration run seeds torch and numpy with the run seed and uses default PyTorch Linear initialisation via build_model [setup_explore_seeding]. Exploration runs come at three fidelities: smoke uses seed 0 on fold 0, verify uses seeds 0-2 on folds 0-2, and full uses seeds 0-4 on folds 0-4 [setup_explore_fidelity].

The exploration minibatch runs use SGD with momentum 0.9 and cross-entropy loss at batch 64 [setup_minibatch]. A torch Generator seeded with the run seed reshuffles the batches each epoch, under a linear warmup then cosine decay with warmup_frac 0.03 or 0.05 [setup_minibatch]. Minibatch runs exp_0012, exp_0013, exp_0016 and exp_0017 used lr 0.05, depth 2, hidden 128, weight_decay 0.0001 and 120 epochs with the identity path on [setup_minibatch_config]. The weight-decay and width arms exp_0021 to exp_0024 also used lr 0.05, and weight_decay 0.0004 was the highest value run [setup_minibatch_config].

All weight-decay and width arms use the warmup-0.05 minibatch script: exp_0024 at hidden 128 with weight_decay 0.0004, exp_0023 at hidden 128 with 0.0004, exp_0021 at hidden 256 with 0.0004, and exp_0022 at hidden 256 with 0.0003 [setup_wd_width_arms]. These arms, exp_0021 to exp_0024, used depth 2 and 120 epochs [setup_wd_width_config]. Runs exp_0014 and exp_0015 used lr 0.05, depth 2, hidden 128, weight_decay 0.0001, 120 epochs and warmup_frac 0.03 with the identity path on [setup_wd_width_config].

sections.heading: Results: Matched Protocol
sections.body:
At the lower shared learning rate, over twenty paired seeds, the plain arm scored 3.6363 and the identity-skip arm scored 2.906 [claim_protocol_lr002]. The paired difference (plain minus identity) has mean 0.73037, median 0.6945 and seed SD 0.562533 [claim_protocol_lr002]. The identity arm was lower on seventeen seeds, tied on three and higher on none [claim_protocol_lr002].

At the higher shared learning rate, over twenty paired seeds, the plain arm scored 2.697 and the identity-skip arm scored 2.5756 [claim_protocol_lr005]. The paired difference (plain minus identity) has mean 0.121405, median 0.0 and seed SD 0.532522 [claim_protocol_lr005]. The identity arm was lower on seven seeds, tied on ten and higher on three [claim_protocol_lr005].

Moving from the lower to the higher shared learning rate lowered error more in the plain arm than in the identity arm [claim_lr_sensitivity]. The plain-arm paired difference (higher minus lower rate) has mean -0.93936, with eighteen seeds lower, two tied and none higher [claim_lr_sensitivity]. The identity-arm paired difference has mean -0.330395, with fourteen seeds lower, three tied and three higher [claim_lr_sensitivity]. All four protocol arms scored below the depth-one full-batch reference arm, which scored 4.2454 [claim_lr_sensitivity].

Judged by the registered rule, the protocol neither supports nor falsifies H1 [claim_protocol_verdict]. At the higher learning rate the mean paired difference lies inside the registered margin, but the engine recorded no interval, so equivalence is not established [claim_protocol_verdict]. At the lower learning rate the mean paired difference already exceeds the margin, so the registered prediction fails there [claim_protocol_verdict]. The registered one-rate attribution cannot be applied, because it presupposes an interval that was not computed [claim_protocol_verdict].

sections.heading: Results: Exploration
sections.body:
The single-seed full-batch exploration contrasts point the same way or not at all [claim_skip_effect_unresolved]. At the lower exploration learning rate, the identity-path arm scored 3.4722 against 5.2083 for the plain arm [claim_skip_effect_unresolved]. At the higher exploration learning rate, both arms scored 4.5139 [claim_skip_effect_unresolved]. That pair gives one seed-zero contrast favouring the identity path and one exact tie, and neither is replicated, so these runs leave the skip effect unresolved [claim_skip_effect_unresolved].

At the higher full-batch exploration learning rate on seed zero, the plain arm and two identity-path runs all scored 4.5139 [claim_fullbatch_lr01_seed0]. The two identity-path runs use scripts that perform the same computation and differ only in how the skip is switched on, so their agreement shows deterministic code, not independent replication [claim_fullbatch_lr01_seed0]. The plain arm's three-seed mean at this rate was 3.8235 [claim_fullbatch_lr01_seed0]. No identity-path run with more than one seed exists at this rate [claim_fullbatch_lr01_seed0].

With the identity path held fixed, reshuffled minibatch SGD with warmup and cosine decay gave five-seed means of 2.7841 and 2.7838 for two warmup fractions, against 3.758 for full-batch training [claim_minibatch_vs_fullbatch]. Every seed was lower in both minibatch runs [claim_minibatch_vs_fullbatch]. Three-seed runs of the two minibatch implementations scored 2.5495 and 2.5491 [claim_minibatch_vs_fullbatch]. The change bundles step count, gradient noise and learning-rate schedule, so it cannot be attributed to any one of them [claim_minibatch_vs_fullbatch].

Raising weight decay to the top of its range in the minibatch regime gave a five-seed mean of 2.575 against 2.7838 [claim_weight_decay]. Seeds zero, two and four fell (2.4306 to 2.0833, 2.439 to 2.0906, 4.5296 to 4.1812), and seeds one and three were unchanged [claim_weight_decay]. Changing only the warmup fraction moves seed zero between 2.4306 and 2.0833 and seed two between 2.439 and 2.7875 [claim_weight_decay]. Those warmup-driven changes are of the same size as the weight-decay changes, so the drop cannot be attributed to weight decay [claim_weight_decay].

At matched weight decay on three seeds, the wider network scored 2.3176 against 2.3172 for the narrower one [claim_width]. The wider network was lower on seed zero (1.7361 versus 2.0833), equal on seed one (2.7778) and higher on seed two (2.439 versus 2.0906) [claim_width]. The width contrast is therefore mixed, with no net change [claim_width]. A wider run that also lowered weight decay gave identical per-seed scores of 1.7361, 2.7778 and 2.439 [claim_width].

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.body:
One explanation fits the pattern: the identity path speeds optimisation under the fixed step budget, so its advantage is largest where the plain arm trains more slowly, at the lower learning rate [claim_mechanism_speed]. The same account would explain why the identity arm is less sensitive to learning rate [claim_mechanism_speed]. This explanation is untested [claim_mechanism_speed]. No validation curves or training-loss logs are in the record, and a slower-converging plain arm and a genuine endpoint effect would produce the same final-error data [claim_mechanism_speed].

The two arms differ in learning-rate sensitivity, so the path and the learning rate interact [limit_17]. The registered rule, which attributes an effect at one learning rate to learning-rate sensitivity, cannot cleanly separate the two [limit_17].

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.body:
The engine computed only mean paired differences, and no TOST, no 90% interval and no bootstrap were computed [limit_1]. The protocol also used twenty seeds rather than the registered thirty [limit_1]. The verdict is therefore descriptive and cannot declare equivalence at either learning rate [limit_1]. The validation fold has about 288 images, so one image moves error by about 0.35 pp [limit_2]. Many paired differences are exact ties or single-image changes, which is close to the registered margin [limit_2].

Residual arms are scored through an exported width-256 Linear/ReLU stack that re-expresses the trained width-128 residual network [limit_3]. Equivalence is asserted in-script, but float summation order may flip rare ties [limit_3]. The DIAG logs are not in the dossier: init and data-order hashes, step counts, skip activation, export max_abs_diff and activation norms [limit_4]. The protocol's void conditions therefore cannot be checked from the record [limit_4].

No per-epoch validation curves exist, so speed cannot be separated from endpoint error [limit_5]. The optimisation-speed explanation therefore remains a hypothesis [limit_5]. A competing explanation is that the plain arm is under-converged at the lower learning rate [limit_5]. Seeds and folds are coupled, because each seed is paired with a fold in a fixed cycle [limit_6]. As a result, seed and fold effects cannot be separated, and the twenty observations may be dependent [limit_6].

Within the protocol, the residual arm differs from the plain arm in its initial function, because the skip is active from step zero, and not only in its trajectory [limit_7]. Learning rate was shared rather than tuned per arm [limit_7]. In the exploration runs, the identity path sits inside the ReLU as a weight reparametrisation (W = I + W'), which is not the protocol's additive skip [limit_8]. In that reparametrisation, weight decay pulls the weights toward identity rather than zero [limit_8].

The two seed-zero identity-path runs at the higher full-batch learning rate agree because the code is identical and deterministic [limit_9]. Neither script logs parametrisation registration, so that it took effect is inferred from the code and from the lower-rate difference [limit_9].

The minibatch-versus-full-batch gain is descriptive across five paired seed/fold pairs with no significance test [limit_10]. No full-batch control with a matched step count separates gradient noise from step count [limit_10]. The weight-decay per-seed changes match warmup-only changes in size [limit_11]. No training error was logged, so the overfitting premise behind the weight-decay change is untested [limit_11].

Width is isolated only at weight decay 0.0004, on three seeds (exp_0021 versus exp_0023) [limit_12]. exp_0022 changes width and weight decay jointly, and no five-seed width result exists [limit_12]. Identical per-seed scores at weight decay 0.0003 and 0.0004 may be coincidences of the coarse metric [limit_13]. No saved artifact config was checked to confirm which weight decay was applied [limit_13].

Results come from one dataset, one depth and one width family [limit_14]. Nothing here generalises to deeper networks, other datasets or normalised residual networks [limit_14]. Current engine source is not proof of historical execution, and legacy exploration records may lack code, data or environment snapshots [limit_15]. The record does not count runs that failed, were killed under the time budget, timed out or were voided [limit_16]. It lists each recorded run as kept or discarded and gives the training attempts of each protocol arm, and nothing further can be recovered [limit_16].

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.body:
We asked whether, in a shallow ReLU MLP on sklearn-digits, a zero-parameter identity skip path changes final validation error relative to a weight-identical plain MLP once parameters, initial weights, minibatch order, step count and a shared learning rate are matched [scope_question].

At the lower shared learning rate, the identity-skip arm scored below the plain arm over twenty paired seeds, with a mean paired difference (plain minus identity) of 0.73037 [claim_protocol_lr002]. The identity arm was lower on seventeen seeds and higher on none [claim_protocol_lr002]. At the higher shared learning rate, the mean paired difference shrank to 0.121405, with a median of 0.0 and ten tied seeds [claim_protocol_lr005].

Raising the shared learning rate lowered error more in the plain arm (mean paired difference -0.93936) than in the identity arm (mean paired difference -0.330395) [claim_lr_sensitivity]. Judged by the registered rule, the protocol neither supports nor falsifies H1, because no interval was recorded at the higher rate and the mean paired difference already exceeds the margin at the lower rate [claim_protocol_verdict].

No per-epoch validation curves exist, so the optimisation-speed explanation remains a hypothesis against the competing account that the plain arm is under-converged at the lower learning rate [limit_5]. The engine computed no TOST, no 90% interval and no bootstrap, and the protocol used twenty seeds rather than the registered thirty, so the verdict is descriptive and cannot declare equivalence at either learning rate [limit_1].

review.title: Does a Zero-Parameter Identity Skip Change Final Error in a Shallow MLP? A Matched-Arm Test on sklearn-digits

reviews.summary:
The paper asks whether a zero-parameter identity skip changes final validation error in a two-block, width-128 ReLU MLP on sklearn-digits. The control is a plain MLP with the same parameters, initial weights, minibatch order, step count and a shared learning rate. Twenty paired seeds were run at two shared learning rates (0.02 and 0.05) with constant-LR minibatch SGD.

The main results:
- At lr 0.02 the identity arm is lower by a mean of 0.73 pp (17 of 20 seeds lower, none higher).
- At lr 0.05 the gap shrinks to 0.12 pp (median 0, 10 ties).
- Raising the LR helps the plain arm more than the identity arm.

The authors decline to give a verdict on H1 because no interval was computed. A long exploration section on full-batch versus minibatch training, weight decay and width is appended; it is mostly unrelated to the question.

The limitations section is unusually candid. However, the study does not deliver the answer its own data could give. The main effect is also plausibly an under-training artifact of a constant-LR, fixed-epoch recipe. The question and technique are well explored, and the setting is a single tiny dataset.
strengths: The paired design is genuinely matched: identical initial weights, identical per-epoch permutations from a generator seeded with 1000003 plus the seed, identical fold per seed index, and a code diff between train.py v7 and v8 limited to the SKIP flag. This is the right way to isolate a zero-parameter architectural change.

Per-seed sign counts are reported alongside means, medians and seed SDs (e.g. 17/3/0 at lr 0.02 and 7/10/3 at lr 0.05). This gives the reader more than a single mean, and the ties expose the coarse metric.

The draft is honest about its deviations from the registered plan: 20 instead of 30 seeds, no per-arm LR tuning, a two-value LR grid, and no TOST. The deviations are listed explicitly in Setup rather than hidden.

The authors explicitly refuse to over-interpret the exploration runs. For example, they note that exp_0007 and exp_0008 agree because of deterministic identical code rather than replication, and that the minibatch gain bundles step count, noise and schedule.
weaknesses:
Results: Matched Protocol and Abstract, on "the engine recorded no interval, so equivalence is not established" and "the registered one-rate attribution cannot be applied". The interval is derivable from numbers the paper itself reports.
- lr 0.05: with mean 0.1214, SD 0.5325 and n = 20, a paired-t 90% interval is roughly [-0.09, +0.33], inside the ±0.5 margin.
- lr 0.02: with mean 0.7304 and SD 0.5625, it is roughly [+0.51, +0.95], just outside the margin.
Under the registered rule (modulo the seed/fold dependence caveat), this reads as equivalence at 0.05 and an effect at 0.02 only, which the rule attributes to LR sensitivity. The headline 'neither supports nor falsifies' is therefore an artifact of not running a one-line computation. Fix: report the paired-t interval and a fold-blocked bootstrap or permutation interval, then apply the rule as registered.

Results and Discussion, on the 0.73 pp gap at lr 0.02. The most parsimonious reading is that the plain arm is simply under-trained at lr 0.02 under 120 epochs at constant LR.
- plain_lr002 scores 3.64%, essentially the logistic-regression baseline of 3.8%.
- The plain arm improves by 0.94 pp when the LR is raised.
The paper names this competing account but supplies no evidence against it. Fix: log training loss and validation error per epoch; or train to convergence (or to a matched training-loss threshold); or add a cosine schedule so that endpoint error is not a proxy for speed.

Setup, on the shared-LR design and the dropped per-arm tuning. The registered plan tuned LR per arm from {0.01, …, 0.2} precisely to avoid comparing one arm at a suboptimal LR. With only two values, and the plain arm still improving at the top of the grid, the sentence "lowered error more in the plain arm" cannot be read as a sensitivity property. It may only mean that 0.05 is closer to the plain arm's optimum. Fix: sweep at least {0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} for both arms and compare at each arm's best LR and across the curve.

Abstract and Introduction, on "All four protocol arms scored below the depth-one full-batch reference arm at 4.2454". The reference differs in depth, optimiser regime (full-batch, one step per epoch) and step count. The comparison carries no information about the skip. The claim that it 'anchors the paired differences' is never explained, since nothing is computed relative to it. Fix: cut the sentence from the Abstract, or define what the anchor is for.

Abstract, on "weight-identical plain MLP ... once ... initial weights ... are matched". The paper later concedes (Limitations) that the residual arm computes a different function from step zero. This means 'matched' means matched parameters, not matched initial behaviour. Fix: state this in the Abstract, and consider a control that equalises initial output scale, e.g. a scaled skip or a zero-initialised branch.

Introduction, fourth contribution, and the whole Results: Exploration section. The minibatch-versus-full-batch, weight-decay and width runs do not bear on the skip question. They use a different identity mechanism (reparametrisation inside the ReLU) and are all inconclusive by the authors' own account. Listing them as a contribution inflates the paper. Fix: move them to an appendix, or drop them.

Limitations, on seeds coupled to folds. With 20 seeds cycling through 5 folds, there are effectively 4 replicates per fold, and fold-level variance enters every paired difference. The analysis treats the 20 differences as independent. Fix: report per-fold mean differences, use a fold-stratified test, or cross seeds fully with folds.

Results, on reporting precision. Differences are reported as 0.73037, 0.121405, -0.93936 and so on, while one image equals 0.35 pp and half the lr 0.05 pairs are exact ties. Fix: round to about 0.01 pp. Also report a continuous metric such as validation log-loss, so the paired test is not dominated by discretisation.

Sign convention. The registered prediction is stated as resid − plain, while all results are reported as plain − resid. This invites sign errors when readers apply the rule. Fix: use one convention throughout.

Significance and originality. That an identity skip eases optimisation and interacts with learning rate is well known. Showing this on one 8x8 dataset, at one depth and one width, without convergence diagnostics does not change practitioner behaviour. The non-obvious finding would be equivalence at convergence, but that was not tested.
questions: Can you report the paired-t 90% intervals and a fold-blocked bootstrap interval computed from the existing per-seed differences, and state the registered-rule verdict that follows from them?
Do the training loss of plain_lr002 and its validation error still decrease at epoch 120? If you train both arms to convergence, or add a cosine schedule, does the lr 0.02 gap persist?
What is each arm's best validation error over a wider shared-LR grid (e.g. up to 0.2)? Does the gap at each arm's optimum fall inside ±0.5 pp?
What exactly does the depth-one reference arm 'anchor', given that no reported quantity is computed relative to it?
Were the DIAG checks (init hashes, data-order hashes, step counts, export max_abs_diff) actually run and passed? If so, can the logs be included so the void conditions can be verified?
Why are 20 seeds mapped onto 5 folds in a fixed cycle rather than fully crossed? What is the per-fold breakdown of the lr 0.02 effect?
Is the 20% held-out test split ever evaluated? If not, why reserve it?

reviews.summary:
The paper asks whether a zero-parameter identity skip changes final validation top-1 error in a two-block, width-128 ReLU MLP on sklearn-digits. Each plain arm is paired with a skip arm on 20 seeds, with matched initial weights, minibatch order and step count, at two shared learning rates (0.02 and 0.05).

At lr 0.02 the skip arm is lower by a mean of 0.73 pp: 17 seeds lower, 3 tied, none higher. At lr 0.05 the mean gap is 0.12 pp, with a median of 0 and 10 ties. The plain arm benefits more from the higher learning rate.

The authors declare H1 neither supported nor falsified, because no interval was computed. They also append single-seed and few-seed exploration runs on minibatch versus full-batch training, weight decay and width.

The write-up is careful about its own limitations. However:
- The verdict is left open by choice rather than necessity. The intervals follow directly from the reported means and SDs.
- The setting is a toy at the smallest possible scale.
- The one positive finding is most plausibly an under-convergence artefact of a fixed 120-epoch constant-lr budget, which the paper itself cannot rule out.
- Roughly half the paper is exploration material that does not bear on the question.

The result would not change what any practitioner does.
strengths: The plain and skip arms share initial weights, minibatch permutation (a Generator seeded with 1000003+seed) and step count. This is a cleaner control than most skip ablations.

Per-seed sign counts are reported alongside means, medians and seed SDs (17/3/0 at lr 0.02; 7/10/3 at lr 0.05). These let a reader judge the discreteness of the effect against the ~0.35 pp single-image resolution.
Deviations from the pre-registration are stated explicitly in Setup: 20 rather than 30 seeds, no per-arm lr tuning, a two-value grid, and no TOST.

The Limitations section is unusually candid about several problems: seed–fold coupling, missing DIAG logs, the export-based scoring of residual arms, and the non-equivalence of the exploration reparametrisation (W=I+W') to the protocol's additive skip.
weaknesses:
**Results: Matched Protocol / Abstract — the verdict is avoidable.**
- The claim: "The registered one-rate attribution cannot be applied, because it presupposes an interval that was not computed."
- The interval follows trivially from numbers already in the paper.
  - lr 0.02: mean 0.730, SD 0.563, n=20 gives a paired-t 90% CI of about [0.51, 0.95], which is entirely outside ±0.5 pp.
  - lr 0.05: mean 0.121, SD 0.533 gives about [-0.09, 0.33], which is entirely inside the margin.
- Applied as registered, the rule therefore attributes the effect to learning-rate sensitivity rather than leaving the question open.
- The paper withholds a conclusion its own data almost decide.
- Fix: compute the paired t/TOST intervals, plus a fold-clustered bootstrap given the seed–fold coupling, and state the rule's outcome.

**Setup / Limitations — fold reuse undercuts n=20.**
- The text says "Folds cycle through 1, 2, 3, 4, 0". So the 20 'independent' pairs use only 5 distinct validation sets of ~288 images each.
- The effective sample for between-fold variation is 5, not 20, and the SD-based reasoning above is optimistic.
- Fix: analyse with fold as a blocking or cluster factor, or decouple seeds from folds.

**Setup — held-out test split is never used.**
- The setup says "A fixed stratified 20% test split is held out", yet every number is validation-fold error.
- The exploration choices (minibatch, schedule, lr range) were made on these same folds.
- Fix: report test-split error for the four protocol arms.

**Discussion / Limitations — the positive finding is confounded with convergence.**
- The paper offers: "the identity path speeds optimisation under the fixed step budget".
- A competing account fits equally well: at lr 0.02 with a constant rate, 120 epochs and no schedule, the plain arm is simply under-trained.
  - The plain arm at lr 0.02 (3.64%) is barely better than the logistic-regression baseline (3.8%).
  - The plain arm drops 0.94 pp when lr rises to 0.05.
- With no training-loss or validation curves, the only non-null result plausibly reflects the training budget rather than the architecture. It would also be unsurprising.
- Fix: log per-epoch train loss and validation error, and extend training or tune lr per arm as originally registered, to check whether the lr-0.02 gap closes at convergence.

**Abstract / Introduction — 'weight-identical' overstates the control.**
- The abstract says the skip is compared against "a weight-identical plain MLP".
- Limitations concedes the arms compute different functions from step zero.
- The residual arm is also scored through an exported width-256 stack, not the trained network.
- Fix: rephrase as 'parameter-count and initialisation matched', and report the export max_abs_diff values.

**Setup — the reference arm is mis-described.**
- The setup states the reference arm "anchors the paired differences". But no paired difference uses it.
- It is a depth-one, full-batch arm with a different optimiser regime, so "All four protocol arms scored below the depth-one full-batch reference arm at 4.2454" is uninformative about skips.
- Fix: either drop the reference arm or state what inference it supports. The logistic-regression baseline is the more meaningful anchor.

**Sign convention.**
- The registered prediction is stated as (resid − plain), while all results are reported as (plain − resid).
- This invites misreading against the registered margin.
- Fix: use one convention throughout.

**Exploration / Introduction (fourth contribution) — exploration is presented as a contribution.**
- Exploration runs are counted as a contribution even though they use a different architecture (depth 2 vs depth 3), a different skip (a reparametrisation inside the ReLU) and a different optimiser (warmup + cosine schedule).
- They are single- or few-seed, and the text itself concludes that none of them can be attributed to anything.
- They add length without evidence on the question.
- Fix: move them to an appendix and remove them from the contributions list.

**Results: Exploration (width) — possible configuration error.**
- The text reports "identical per-seed scores of 1.7361, 2.7778 and 2.439" at weight decay 0.0003 and 0.0004.
- Identical scores across three seeds strongly suggest weight decay was not actually varied.
- exp_0023 and exp_0024 are also listed with identical configurations without explanation.
- Fix: verify the saved configs or drop the claim.

**Significance / originality.**
- The setting is a single toy dataset, one depth and one width family, with a 2-layer-block MLP where skip effects are known to be minor.
- The question as posed (does a skip matter at shallow depth?) has a widely expected answer: little, and lr-dependent.
- Nothing here would change practice.
- Fix: requires multiple datasets/depths and properly computed equivalence tests, at minimum.

**Related Work — misrepresentation and padding.**
- The claim that RoR "reports accuracy gains without a matched no-shortcut ablation" needs a citation-level check.
- The capsule-network reference is self-admittedly peripheral and carries no abstract. It is decoration and should be cut.

reviews.summary:
The paper tests whether a zero-parameter identity skip changes final validation error in a two-block, width-128 ReLU MLP on sklearn-digits. The design pairs plain and skip arms on 20 seeds with matched initial weights, minibatch order and step count, at two shared learning rates (0.02 and 0.05).

- At lr 0.02 the skip arm is better by a mean of 0.73 pp (SD 0.56; lower on 17 seeds, tied on 3, higher on none).
- At lr 0.05 the gap shrinks to 0.12 pp (median 0, 10 ties).
- The plain arm gains more from the higher learning rate, so skip and learning rate interact.

The authors declare the registered rule inapplicable because no interval was computed, and give no verdict. A long exploration section on full-batch vs minibatch training, weight decay and width is reported as non-confirmatory.

The write-up is careful and candid about its limits. However, the contribution is small: one dataset, one depth, two learning rates. The headline pattern is that a skip helps where the plain network is under-trained and washes out at a better learning rate, which is what one would predict. The non-verdict is also self-imposed, since the reported mean, SD and n are enough to compute the registered interval.
strengths: The matched-arm design isolates the skip path itself: identical initial weights, shared per-epoch permutation generator (1000003 + seed), identical step count and the same fold per seed index across arms (Setup and Protocol).
Effect direction is reported per seed (17/3/0 at lr 0.02; 7/10/3 at lr 0.05) alongside mean, median and SD. With a 0.35 pp metric quantum this is more informative than a mean alone.
Deviations from the pre-registration are disclosed explicitly: 20 instead of 30 seeds, no per-arm learning-rate tuning, two learning rates, descriptive statistics instead of TOST.

The paper disciplines its own exploration results. It notes that the two seed-zero identity runs at lr 0.1 agreeing at 4.5139 reflects deterministic code, not replication. It also notes that warmup-only changes match the weight-decay changes in size, so the weight-decay drop is not attributed.

The learning-rate × skip interaction (plain arm improves by 0.94 pp from lr 0.02 to 0.05, skip arm by 0.33 pp; 18/2/0 vs 14/3/3) is a concrete observation. It reframes the question from 'does the skip matter' to 'does the skip matter at a well-tuned learning rate'.
weaknesses:
Self-consistency (Results: Matched Protocol, last paragraph; Abstract, final paragraph): the claim that 'the registered one-rate attribution cannot be applied, because it presupposes an interval that was not computed' does not hold. The interval follows directly from the reported summary statistics.
- lr 0.02: mean 0.730, SD 0.563, n=20 gives SE ≈ 0.126. The 90% t-interval is ≈ [0.51, 0.95], entirely outside ±0.5.
- lr 0.05: mean 0.121, SD 0.533 gives an interval ≈ [−0.09, 0.33], inside the margin.
- Under the registered rule, this is an effect at one learning rate only, attributed to learning-rate sensitivity, i.e. H1 is not falsified.
Fix: compute the paired t-interval or TOST from the stored per-seed values. If seed–fold dependence is the concern, also report a fold-clustered or permutation interval. Then state the verdict.

Overreach in framing (Abstract, Discussion): the lower-rate 'effect' coincides with an under-trained plain arm. Plain at lr 0.02 scores 3.64, barely below the 3.8 logistic-regression baseline in Setup, and well above plain at lr 0.05 (2.70).
- The most parsimonious reading is that the skip compensates for a sub-optimal learning rate under a fixed step budget, not that it changes reachable error.
- The registered plan's per-arm learning-rate tuning (dropped in deviations) was exactly the control for this.
Fix: run per-arm learning-rate selection on the inner split as registered, or at least add lr 0.1. Log training loss and per-epoch validation error so speed can be separated from endpoint error.

Unclear role of the reference arm (Setup: 'The reference arm anchors the paired differences'; Abstract: 'All four protocol arms scored below the depth-one full-batch reference arm at 4.2454').
- The reference arm (depth 1, full-batch, train.py v2) enters no paired difference.
- It differs from the protocol arms in depth, optimiser regime and step count, so the comparison is uninformative about the skip.
Fix: either state what the anchor is used for, or drop the sentence from the Abstract and contributions.

Sign-convention inconsistency (Setup vs Results): the registered prediction is stated as resid − plain, but all results are reported as plain − identity. Readers must flip signs to check the rule.
Fix: report in the registered direction, or state the flip explicitly next to the rule.

Scope of the exploration section (Exploration Runs; Results: Exploration): roughly a third of the paper covers full-batch vs minibatch training, weight decay and width. These are single- to five-seed runs, use a different skip (the W = I + W' reparametrisation inside the ReLU, per Limitations) and a different schedule (warmup + cosine). They do not bear on the protocol question. The width result (2.3176 vs 2.3172 on 3 seeds) and the identical per-seed scores at weight decay 0.0003 vs 0.0004 are noise-level.
Fix: move this material to an appendix and remove contribution 4 from the Introduction.

Statistical dependence (Limitations: 'Seeds and folds are coupled'): 20 seeds over 5 folds means 4 seeds per fold, so per-seed differences are not independent. Fix: report per-fold mean differences, a mixed-effects estimate, or decouple seeds from folds.

Clarity and presentation:
